The story effectively explores the differing socioeconomic and personal perspectives of its three main characters: Nora (a working-class former cashier), Daniel (a privileged, somewhat oblivious interior designer), and Miss Emily (a self-made, controlling businesswoman). Miss Emily, in particular, is a difficult and often abrasive character—critical of how Nora cuts a pear, puts wooden spoons in the dishwasher, or speaks about her past employment. However, her perspective is presented with great depth and conviction. Rather than portraying her as a simple snob or caricature of an overbearing mother-in-law, the story reveals the hard-earned pragmatism behind her behavior—stemming from when her husband abandoned her with seventy-three dollars and a business to run. Her seemingly elitist advice to Nora about not leading with her supermarket job is convincingly framed not as shame, but as a protective desire to give Nora "a moment before they decide" where to place her socially.
